title: Protecting the Ocean
keyIdea: People can protect the ocean. Sustainable fishing means taking only as many fish as can grow back; take more and the fish run out. A marine protected area is a part of the sea where fishing and pollution are limited or banned, so sea life can recover, and fish often spill out into the water around it. Beach clean-ups and using less plastic keep plastic away from animals like turtles. Countries agree to cut the carbon dioxide (CO₂) from burning fuel, because CO₂ soaking into the sea makes it more acidic and harder for animals to build shells.
familyTip: Next time you shop together, count the single-use plastic items in the basket and pick one you could swap for a reusable one. If you buy fish, look for a label that shows it was caught or farmed sustainably, and talk about what that means.

visual.caption: Does this help the ocean or harm it? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: set a fishing catch, add a no-fishing zone, clear a beach of plastic, turn up the CO₂ dial, and match each threat to its fix.

kid: The ocean gives us food. About half of the oxygen made on Earth comes from tiny living things in the sea called plankton. But the ocean faces three big threats: too much fishing, plastic, and the gas carbon dioxide. People are working to fix all three.

Fish grow back, but only so fast. If boats catch more than grow back each year, the fish run out. Sustainable fishing means taking only what the sea can replace. Countries set limits on how many fish boats may catch.

A marine protected area is a part of the sea with strict rules. In a no-fishing zone, nobody may fish. Fish there grow big and have lots of young. Some swim out, so fishing nearby often gets better too.

Plastic washes into the sea from land. A turtle can eat a bag because it looks like a jellyfish. Clean-ups and using less plastic help. Burning fuel adds carbon dioxide to the air, and the sea soaks it up. It makes the water more acidic, so shells are harder to build. Countries have agreed to cut it.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This supports NGSS 5-ESS3-1 (how communities use science ideas to protect Earth's resources and environment) and the National Curriculum in England (Year 4: environments can change and this can pose dangers to living things). It covers four protections: catch limits for sustainable fishing, marine protected areas (MPAs), cutting plastic pollution, and international agreements such as the Paris Agreement that aim to cut carbon dioxide emissions.

The lab has five tasks, all with simple models. The fishing model grows the fish left by a quarter each year up to 100, so 20 a year is sustainable and 30 a year empties the stock in 5 years. The zone model shows spillover: with one no-fishing zone, both the catch and the fish left are higher than with none, matching reviews of fully protected areas where fish biomass is often several times higher inside. The ocean has absorbed about a quarter of the CO₂ released by people, and surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1, about 30% more acidic.

Common mistakes. Learners often think more fishing always means more food, that a protected area must make the nearby catch fall, or that one action like a beach clean-up fixes every threat. Take care with acidification: sea water is still slightly alkaline, so more acidic means its pH is falling, not that the sea has turned into acid.

choices: Taking only as many fish as can grow back
Catching as many fish as you can
Never catching any fish
practice.hint: Think of the catch that kept 100 fish in the sea for 10 years in the lab.
practice.explain: Sustainable fishing takes only what the sea can replace, so there are fish for next year too.

practice.prompt: A bay has 100 fish. Boats catch {c} this year. How many fish are left before they grow back?
practice.hint: Take the catch away from the 100 fish.
practice.explain: 100 − {c} = {=100-c} fish are left to grow back.

practice.prompt: Why do no-fishing zones often help fishing boats nearby?
choices: Fish grow big inside and some swim out
Boats can fish inside the zone at night
The zone pushes all fish away
practice.hint: In the lab, look at the zones next to the no-fishing zone.
practice.explain: Protected fish grow and breed, and some spill out into the water around the zone.

practice.prompt: A class picks up {a} plastic bottles and {b} plastic bags on a beach. How many pieces of plastic is that?
practice.hint: Add the bottles and the bags.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} pieces of plastic kept out of the sea.

practice.prompt: What makes the sea more acidic?
choices: Carbon dioxide from burning fuel soaking into it
Plastic bags
Too many fish
practice.hint: Which gas did the dial in the lab turn up?
practice.explain: Burning coal, oil and gas adds CO₂ to the air. The sea soaks it up and gets more acidic.

pool.prompt: What is a marine protected area?
choices: A part of the sea where fishing and pollution are limited or banned
A swimming area with lifeguards
A tank where fish are kept
pool.hint: It is a real part of the sea, with rules.
pool.explain: A marine protected area has rules that limit fishing and pollution so sea life can recover.

pool.prompt: Fish grow back by {g} each year in a lake. To fish sustainably, what is the most you should catch each year?
pool.hint: Take no more than the sea or lake can replace.
pool.explain: Catch at most {g} a year, the same as grow back, and the number of fish stays steady.

pool.prompt: A turtle eats a plastic bag. Why?
choices: The bag looks like a jellyfish
Turtles like the taste of plastic
The bag is warm
pool.hint: What do sea turtles hunt for food?
pool.explain: Leatherback and other turtles eat jellyfish. A floating bag looks just like one.

pool.prompt: Which action helps stop the sea getting more acidic?
choices: Burning less coal, oil and gas
A beach clean-up
Bigger fishing nets
pool.hint: Acid sea comes from a gas in the air.
pool.explain: Less fuel burned means less CO₂ in the air, so less soaks into the sea.

pool.prompt: Leo says a no-fishing zone must make the catch nearby fall. What is right?
choices: Nearby catches often go up, as fish swim out
Leo is right
All the fish leave the zone
pool.hint: Remember the two runs in the lab.
pool.explain: In the lab and in many real areas, fish spill out of the zone, so nearby catches can rise.

pool.prompt: A school uses {n} plastic bottles a week. It switches to refill bottles. How many plastic bottles does it save in 2 weeks?
pool.hint: Each week saves {n} bottles. There are 2 weeks.
pool.explain: {n} × 2 = {=2*n} bottles kept out of the bin and the sea.

pool.prompt: Why do countries sign agreements like the Paris Agreement?
choices: To cut the CO₂ that warms the planet and makes the sea acidic
To share fishing nets
To build more beaches
pool.hint: No one country can cut world CO₂ alone.
pool.explain: CO₂ mixes all round the world, so countries agree together to cut it.

choices: Catching more fish each year than grow back
Catching a few fish for dinner
Fishing only outside a no-fishing zone
pool.hint: What happened at 30 fish a year in the lab?
pool.explain: Overfishing takes more than grows back, so the fish get fewer every year until they run out.
